## Getting Started (AngleSharp.Wasm)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/general/basics/
> Project: AngleSharp.Wasm (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Wasm)
> Package: AngleSharp.Wasm 1.1.1 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Wasm`
> Docs revision: 1044be7bc91ea340a048447d74634ebb7b0d909a

### Requirements

AngleSharp.Wasm currently targets modern .NET runtimes and is available for .NET 8 and .NET 10.

You need to have AngleSharp installed already. This could be done via NuGet:

```ps1
Install-Package AngleSharp
```

If you want JavaScript-side access to `window.WebAssembly`, you also need a scripting setup (for example, AngleSharp.Js) that discovers exported DOM members from loaded assemblies.

### Getting AngleSharp.Wasm over NuGet

The simplest way of integrating AngleSharp.Wasm to your project is by using NuGet. You can install AngleSharp.Wasm by opening the package manager console (PM) and typing in the following statement:

```ps1
Install-Package AngleSharp.Wasm
```

You can also use the graphical library package manager ("Manage NuGet Packages for Solution"). Searching for "AngleSharp.Wasm" in the official NuGet online feed will find this library.

### Setting up AngleSharp.Wasm

To use AngleSharp.Wasm you need to add it to your `Configuration` coming from AngleSharp itself.

If you just want a configuration *that works* you should use the following code:

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default
    .WithWasm(); // from AngleSharp.Wasm
```

This will register everything related for running WebAssembly.

### Optional: Register Host Imports

If your Wasm module imports host functions, register import providers:

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default
        .WithWasm()
        .WithWasmImports(context =>
        {
                return new[]
                {
                        new WasmImportFunction(
                                moduleName: "host",
                                functionName: "answer",
                                parameterTypes: Array.Empty<WasmValueType>(),
                                resultTypes: new[] { WasmValueType.Int32 },
                                callback: _ => 41),
                };
        });
```

### What Works Today

- `WithWasm()` registers a default Wasmtime-backed runtime factory.
- `WithWasmImports(...)` can provide host imports during instantiation.
- The DOM surface exposes `WebAssembly.compile(...)` and `WebAssembly.instantiate(...)`.
- `Module` metadata APIs are available:
    - `exports()`
    - `imports()`
    - `customSections(sectionName)`
- `Instance` supports:
    - `exports` object access by name
    - `invoke(exportName, ...args)` helper
- Export descriptors expose spec-style fields (`name`, `kind`).

### Current Limitations

AngleSharp.Wasm currently implements a pragmatic subset of the WebAssembly JS API.

- Synchronous bridge calls are used (`compile` / `instantiate` are not Promise-based APIs).
- Streaming APIs synchronously buffer AngleSharp response streams. Compile options are forwarded to capable runtimes, but Wasmtime 44 does not support JavaScript string builtins or imported string constants.
- `Instance.exports` function members are wrapper objects requiring `.invoke(...)`.
- Compile, link, and execution failures are projected as `CompileError`, `LinkError`, and `RuntimeError` objects.
- Exported memories, tables, globals, and tags have object projections; other non-function exports remain descriptors (`name`, `kind`).
- Host-created exceptions support tag identity and typed payload inspection. The default Wasmtime 44 backend does not expose native Tag or Exception handles, so runtime-thrown Wasm exceptions are not yet projected.
- `customSections(...)` returns payload bytes (`byte[]`) mapped from custom sections.
- Runtime invocation/import marshaling is currently focused on numeric value kinds (`i32`, `i64`, `f32`, `f64`).

These limitations are intentional for the current release scope and can be evolved incrementally.


---

## Spec Coverage Matrix (AngleSharp.Wasm)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/general/spec-coverage/
> Project: AngleSharp.Wasm (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Wasm)
> Package: AngleSharp.Wasm 1.1.1 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Wasm`
> Docs revision: 1044be7bc91ea340a048447d74634ebb7b0d909a

This page maps the current AngleSharp.Wasm implementation to the WebAssembly JavaScript API specification.

Status values:

- Implemented: Available and intended for normal use.
- Partial: Available in a reduced or adapted form.
- Not yet: Not currently implemented.

### Coverage Table

| Spec Area | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WebAssembly namespace: `compile(bytes)` | Implemented | `WebAssembly.compile(bytes)` gives a promise of a `WebAssembly.Module`, rejected with a `CompileError` for invalid bytes. The synchronous `WebAssembly.Compile(window, bytes)` remains for C#. |
| WebAssembly namespace: `instantiate(...)` | Implemented | `WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, importObject)` gives a promise of `{ module, instance }`, `instantiate(module, importObject)` one of the instance. Imports are read from the import object (functions, numbers, BigInts, memories, tables and globals); failures reject with a `LinkError` or `RuntimeError`. |
| WebAssembly namespace: `validate(bytes)` | Implemented | Exposed as synchronous `WebAssembly.validate(byte[])`, using native Wasmtime validation or compile-and-dispose fallback for custom runtimes. |
| WebAssembly namespace: streaming APIs | Implemented | `compileStreaming` and `instantiateStreaming` take a `Response` of `fetch()` (or a promise of one, or an AngleSharp `IResponse`), which has to be successful and of the type `application/wasm`; the body is read completely before compiling. |
| WebAssembly namespace: compile options | Partial | `WasmCompileOptions` validates and routes `builtins` and `importedStringConstants` through compile, byte instantiate, and streaming entry points. Wasmtime 44 cannot execute these options. |
| `Module.exports(module)` | Implemented | `WebAssembly.Module.exports(module)` gives descriptor objects (`name`, `kind`). |
| `Module.imports(module)` | Implemented | `WebAssembly.Module.imports(module)` gives descriptor objects (`module`, `name`, `kind`). |
| `Module.customSections(module, name)` | Implemented | `WebAssembly.Module.customSections(module, name)` gives ArrayBuffers. |
| `Instance.exports` | Implemented | An object with the exports in the order of the module: functions scripts call (the same function for the same export), and `WebAssembly.Memory`, `Table` and `Global` objects. `new WebAssembly.Instance(module, importObject)` instantiates synchronously. |
| Exported function invocation | Implemented | Exported functions are functions of scripts, converting their arguments and results as the standard says (`i64` as BigInt); a trap is a `RuntimeError`, and what a function of a script imported by the module threw reaches the caller as it is. |
| Host import functions | Implemented | Functions of scripts in the import object, and C# functions via `WithWasmImports(...)` and `WasmImportFunction`. |
| Memory object API (`Memory`) | Implemented | `new WebAssembly.Memory({ initial, maximum })`, imports and exports. With the default Wasmtime backend `buffer` is an ArrayBuffer sharing the bytes of the memory (the memories are pinned .NET arrays, via Wasmtime's host memory creator), which is a new one after the memory has grown. Shared memories are not supported. |
| Table object API (`Table`) | Implemented | `new WebAssembly.Table({ element, initial, maximum })`, imports and exports, with `length`, `get(index)`, `set(index, value)` and `grow(delta, value)`. |
| Global object API (`Global`) | Implemented | `new WebAssembly.Global({ value, mutable }, value)`, imports (also of numbers and BigInts) and exports, with `value` and `valueOf()`. |
| Tag object API (`Tag`) | Partial | Host-created and exported tags expose `type().parameters`, including re-exported imported tags. Wasmtime 44 does not expose native Tag handles or enable exception modules through its .NET API. |
| Exception object API (`Exception`) | Partial | Host-created exceptions validate typed payloads and expose `is(tag)` and `getArg(tag, index)`. Runtime-thrown Wasm exceptions cannot be projected through Wasmtime 44. |
| Error constructors (`CompileError`, `LinkError`, `RuntimeError`) | Implemented | Public DOM-named constructors are available, and compile, instantiate/link, and execution failures are translated at bridge boundaries. |
| JS String builtins set | Partial | The `js-string` builtin set is recognized and forwarded to capable custom runtimes; Wasmtime 44 has no corresponding API. |

### Runtime and Type Support

| Area | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime backend | Implemented | Uses Wasmtime through the default `WithWasm()` registration. |
| Invocation numeric value types | Implemented | `i32`, `i64`, `f32`, `f64` are supported for import/export invocation paths. |
| Extended/reference value kinds | Partial | Table projections support `funcref` and `externref`; broader reference-type invocation marshaling is not yet exposed. |

### Test-Backed Behavior

The current implementation is validated by runtime and bridge tests in the repository, including:

- compile and instantiate flows
- module validation
- response-based compilation and instantiation
- compile option validation and runtime forwarding
- export invocation
- exported memory read, write, and growth
- exported table access, mutation, and growth
- exported global access and mutation
- exported and re-exported tag type metadata
- host-created exception payload validation and inspection
- compile, link, and runtime error translation
- import descriptor extraction
- export descriptor extraction
- custom section lookup behavior
- host import wiring

### Interpretation Notes

This matrix reflects API shape and behavior in AngleSharp.Wasm, not strict one-to-one Web IDL signatures.
Scripts (with AngleSharp.Js) see the API of the standard: `WebAssembly` is a namespace object holding the interfaces (`WebAssembly.Module`, `Instance`, `Memory`, `Table`, `Global`, `Tag`, `Exception` and the errors), and its operations give promises. The synchronous bridge methods remain for C#.


---

## API Documentation (AngleSharp.Wasm)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/tutorials/api/
> Project: AngleSharp.Wasm (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Wasm)
> Package: AngleSharp.Wasm 1.1.1 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Wasm`
> Docs revision: 1044be7bc91ea340a048447d74634ebb7b0d909a

This page summarizes the currently available public API surface.

### Configuration Extensions

Extension methods are available on `IConfiguration` via `AngleSharp.Wasm`:

#### `WithWasm()`

Registers the default Wasmtime-backed runtime factory.

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default.WithWasm();
```

#### `WithWasm(WasmRuntimeOptions)`

Registers the default Wasmtime-backed runtime factory with resource limits. Every limit is off by
default; set them when pages with untrusted WebAssembly are loaded.

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default.WithWasm(new WasmRuntimeOptions
{
    MaximumMemorySize = 64 * 1024 * 1024, // bytes per linear memory
    MaximumTableElements = 10_000,        // elements per table
    Fuel = 100_000_000,                   // per call from the host and per instantiation
});
```

- `MaximumMemorySize` and `MaximumTableElements` make instantiation fail when a memory or table
  starts larger, and make growing beyond them fail.
- `Fuel` is roughly one unit per executed WebAssembly instruction. A call that spends it traps,
  which the bridge reports as `RuntimeError`; the next call gets a full budget again. Calls that
  WebAssembly makes back into its own instance through a host import share the outer call's budget.
  Fuel metering slows execution down, so it is only enabled when `Fuel` is set.

The same options can be passed to `new WasmtimeWasmRuntime(options)` and
`new WasmtimeWasmRuntimeFactory(options)`.

#### `WithWasm(Func<IBrowsingContext, IWasmRuntimeFactory>)`

Registers a custom runtime factory creator.

#### `WithWasmImports(IWasmImportProvider)`

Registers a host import provider.

#### `WithWasmImports(Func<IBrowsingContext, IEnumerable<WasmImportFunction>>)`

Registers host imports via delegate.

### DOM-Facing API (`AngleSharp.Wasm.Dom`)

When used with a scripting integration that discovers DOM attributes, the following surface is exposed under `WebAssembly`.

#### `WebAssembly.compile(byte[] moduleBytes)`

Compiles bytes and returns a `WasmJsModule`.

An overload accepts `WasmCompileOptions`.

#### `WebAssembly.validate(byte[] moduleBytes)`

Returns whether the bytes form a valid WebAssembly module without instantiating it.

#### `WebAssembly.compileStreaming(IResponse source)`

Synchronously consumes a successful `application/wasm` response and returns a compiled `WasmJsModule`.

An overload accepts `WasmCompileOptions`.

#### `WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(IResponse source)`

Synchronously consumes a successful `application/wasm` response and returns a `WasmJsInstantiationResult` containing `module` and `instance`.

An overload accepts `WasmCompileOptions`.

#### `WebAssembly.instantiate(WasmJsModule module)`

Instantiates a compiled module and returns a `WasmJsInstance`.

Byte-array overloads compile and instantiate in one operation and return `WasmJsInstantiationResult`; compile options can be supplied.

### `WasmCompileOptions`

- `builtins`: requested builtin sets; currently the standard `js-string` value is recognized.
- `importedStringConstants`: module namespace for imported string constants.

Options are forwarded to runtimes implementing `IWasmCompileOptionsCompiler`. Wasmtime 44 does not expose either feature and rejects non-empty options.

### `WasmJsModule`

#### `exports()`

Returns `WasmModuleExportDescriptor[]` with:

- `name`
- `kind` (`function`, `table`, `memory`, `global`, `tag`)

#### `imports()`

Returns `WasmModuleImportDescriptor[]` with:

- `module`
- `name`
- `kind`

#### `customSections(string sectionName)`

Returns all matching custom section payloads as `byte[][]`.

### `WasmJsInstance`

#### `exports` (getter)

Returns a `WasmJsExports` object.

#### `invoke(string exportName, params object?[] arguments)`

Invokes an exported function by name.

### `WasmJsExports`

#### `this[string name]`

Returns an export entry by name:

- `WasmJsExportedFunction` for function exports
- `WasmJsMemory` for memory exports
- `WasmJsTable` for table exports
- `WasmJsGlobal` for global exports
- `WasmJsTag` for tag exports
- `WasmJsExportValue` for other non-function exports
- `null` if no export is found

#### `keys()`

Returns all export names.

### `WasmJsExportedFunction`

#### `invoke(params object?[] arguments)`

Invokes the wrapped exported function.

### `WasmJsMemory`

Provides `buffer`, `read(offset, count)`, `write(offset, bytes)`, and `grow(delta)`.

### `WasmJsTable`

Provides `length`, `get(index)`, `set(index, value)`, and `grow(delta, value)`. Function references returned by `get(...)` expose `invoke(...)`.

### `WasmJsGlobal`

Provides a `value` accessor and `valueOf()`. Assigning to an immutable global throws `InvalidOperationException`.

### `WasmJsTag`

Can be constructed with an ordered array of WebAssembly value type names. Provides `type()`, whose descriptor exposes the tag's `parameters`.

### `WasmJsException`

Construct with a `WasmJsTag` and matching payload array. Provides `is(tag)` and `getArg(tag, index)` and can be thrown and caught as a .NET exception. Runtime-thrown Wasm exceptions are not available through the default Wasmtime 44 backend.

### Error Constructors

`WasmJsCompileError`, `WasmJsLinkError`, and `WasmJsRuntimeError` expose the standard `CompileError`, `LinkError`, and `RuntimeError` DOM names. Each can be constructed with an optional message. Bridge compilation, linking, and execution failures are translated automatically.

### `WasmJsExportValue`

Descriptor type for non-function exports.

- `name`
- `kind`

### Notes on Scope

This API is intentionally focused on a practical subset of the full WebAssembly JS API spec. See [Questions](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/tutorials/questions/index.html.md) for limitations and expected behavior.

For a section-by-section status overview, see [Spec Coverage Matrix](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/general/spec-coverage/index.html.md).


---

## Examples (AngleSharp.Wasm)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/tutorials/examples/
> Project: AngleSharp.Wasm (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Wasm)
> Package: AngleSharp.Wasm 1.1.1 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Wasm`
> Docs revision: 1044be7bc91ea340a048447d74634ebb7b0d909a

This is a (growing) list of examples for every-day usage of AngleSharp.Wasm.

### Basic Setup

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default.WithWasm();
using var context = BrowsingContext.New(config);
using var document = await context.OpenNewAsync();
```

### Compile and Instantiate

```cs
var module = WebAssembly.Compile(context.Current!, wasmBytes);
var instance = WebAssembly.Instantiate(context.Current!, module);
```

### Invoke an Exported Function

```cs
var result = instance.Invoke("answer");
```

You can also invoke through the export wrapper:

```cs
var exported = (WasmJsExportedFunction?)instance.Exports["answer"];
var result = exported?.Invoke();
```

### Invoke an Exported Function with Arguments

```cs
var add = (WasmJsExportedFunction?)instance.Exports["add"];
var result = add?.Invoke(20, 22); // 42
```

### Read Module Export and Import Metadata

```cs
foreach (var exportEntry in module.Exports())
{
	Console.WriteLine($"Export: {exportEntry.Name} ({exportEntry.Kind})");
}

foreach (var importEntry in module.Imports())
{
	Console.WriteLine($"Import: {importEntry.Module}.{importEntry.Name} ({importEntry.Kind})");
}
```

### Read Custom Sections

```cs
var sections = module.CustomSections("meta");

foreach (var payload in sections)
{
	Console.WriteLine($"Section payload length: {payload.Length}");
}
```

### Register Host Imports

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default
	.WithWasm()
	.WithWasmImports(_ =>
	{
		return new[]
		{
			new WasmImportFunction(
				"host",
				"answer",
				Array.Empty<WasmValueType>(),
				new[] { WasmValueType.Int32 },
				_ => 41),
		};
	});
```

With a module importing `host.answer`, an export such as `answer_plus_one` can now be invoked as expected.

### Check for Missing Exports

```cs
var maybe = instance.Exports["does_not_exist"];

if (maybe is null)
{
	Console.WriteLine("Export not found.");
}
```

### List Available Export Names

```cs
var keys = instance.Exports.Keys();
```


---

## Questions (AngleSharp.Wasm)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/tutorials/questions/
> Project: AngleSharp.Wasm (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Wasm)
> Package: AngleSharp.Wasm 1.1.1 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Wasm`
> Docs revision: 1044be7bc91ea340a048447d74634ebb7b0d909a

For a compact section-by-section status view, see [Spec Coverage Matrix](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/wasm/general/spec-coverage/index.html.md).

### Which .NET versions are supported?

AngleSharp.Wasm currently targets .NET 8 and .NET 10.

### Is the full WebAssembly JS API specification implemented?

Not yet. The current implementation covers a useful subset with emphasis on:

- Compiling and instantiating modules
- Reading module metadata (`exports`, `imports`, `customSections`)
- Invoking exported functions
- Registering host imports

### Is `window.WebAssembly` available?

Yes, when used with a scripting integration that discovers DOM-annotated members from registered assemblies.

### Are APIs synchronous or asynchronous?

The current bridge methods are synchronous from the caller perspective.

### Are `Memory`, `Table`, `Global`, and `Tag` exposed as JS API objects?

Exported memories, tables, and globals have usable object projections. Host-created and exported tags expose `type().parameters`, including metadata for re-exported imported tags. Host-created exceptions support `is(tag)` and `getArg(tag, index)`. Memory, table, and global construction and imports are not yet exposed.

Wasmtime 44 does not expose native Tag or Exception handles or enable exception modules through its .NET API, so runtime-thrown Wasm exceptions are not yet projected through the default backend.

### How do I invoke exported functions?

Either call:

- `instance.Invoke("exportName", args...)`

or use the export wrapper:

- `((WasmJsExportedFunction)instance.Exports["exportName"]).Invoke(args...)`

### What does `Module.customSections(name)` return?

It returns all matching custom section payloads as `byte[][]`.

### How are host imports provided?

Use `WithWasmImports(...)` with either:

- an `IWasmImportProvider`, or
- a delegate returning `IEnumerable<WasmImportFunction>`.

### Which value kinds are currently supported for invocation/import marshaling?

Current numeric value kinds are supported:

- `i32`
- `i64`
- `f32`
- `f64`

### How do I limit what a module can consume?

By default a module can grow its memory and tables up to the WebAssembly maximum and run for as
long as it likes. Pass `WasmRuntimeOptions` to `WithWasm(...)` to cap memory size, table
elements and fuel (executed instructions per call); see the API page.

### What are known limitations today?

- No Promise-based `compile` / `instantiate` bridge methods.
- Streaming APIs buffer response bodies and return synchronously rather than returning promises.
- Wasmtime 44 cannot execute the `builtins` or `importedStringConstants` compile options; capable custom runtimes can implement them through `IWasmCompileOptionsCompiler`.
- Runtime-thrown Wasm exception interoperability is not yet available.

These limits are expected at this stage and can be expanded in future versions.

## Benchmarks (AngleSharp.Renderer)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/benchmarks/
> Project: AngleSharp.Renderer (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Renderer)
> Package: AngleSharp.Renderer 0.12.0 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Renderer`
> Docs revision: 0a71fb1145856a0e638852edb3b9de0385eb01fa

All benchmarks have been run using .NET 10 on an Apple M5 Pro with 24 GB of memory.

### Baseline (0.5.0)

┌───────────────────────────┬────────┬───────────┐
│           Stage           │  Mean  │ Allocated │
├───────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Parse HTML+CSS            │ 1.2 ms │   1.96 MB │
├───────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Layout (BuildDisplayList) │ 2.42 s │  1,456 MB │
├───────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Full render (RenderToPng) │ 2.67 s │  1,461 MB │
└───────────────────────────┴────────┴───────────┘

### Current (0.6.0)

Three fixes landed, all eliminating redundant work rather than changing what gets rendered:

1. Element style is now cached per render (`GetOrCreateStyleMap`), instead of being recomputed from
   scratch every time a flex/grid item, inline-block prediction, or paint-order check reads the
   same element's style ahead of its own real layout pass.
2. The handful of properties read from the cascaded-but-uncomputed declaration (grid tracks, gap,
   `background-image` - see `ResolveExplicitPropertyValue`'s own remarks) used to rebuild the
   *entire document's* style collection and re-walk the element's full ancestor chain on every one
   of up to 8 calls per element; both are now built/read once per element instead.
3. Grid/flex-container-only properties (`grid-template-columns`/`-rows`, `gap` and friends,
   `flex-direction`/`justify-content`/`align-items`/`flex-wrap`/`align-content`) are no longer read
   at all for an element that provably cannot be a grid/flex container itself.

Combined, layout allocates ~7.5x less and runs ~9.5x faster than the original (0.5.0) baseline;
full render time (layout + rasterization + PNG encoding) follows closely behind, since
rasterization/encoding was always a small, roughly fixed slice of total time. See
`src/AngleSharp.Renderer.Benchmarks/BASELINE.md` for the full before/after breakdown of each fix.

┌───────────────────────────┬────────┬───────────┐
│           Stage           │  Mean  │ Allocated │
├───────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Parse HTML+CSS            │ 1.5 ms │   1.96 MB │
├───────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Layout (BuildDisplayList) │ 0.26 s │    194 MB │
├───────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Full render (RenderToPng) │ 0.48 s │    199 MB │
└───────────────────────────┴────────┴───────────┘


---

## Getting Started (AngleSharp.Renderer)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/general/basics/
> Project: AngleSharp.Renderer (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Renderer)
> Package: AngleSharp.Renderer 0.12.0 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Renderer`
> Docs revision: 0a71fb1145856a0e638852edb3b9de0385eb01fa

### Requirements

AngleSharp.Renderer builds on top of AngleSharp and AngleSharp.Css. Install the packages you need via NuGet:

```ps1
Install-Package AngleSharp
Install-Package AngleSharp.Css
Install-Package AngleSharp.Renderer
```

### Rendering Pipeline

The renderer works in three steps:

1. AngleSharp parses the HTML document.
2. AngleSharp.Css provides computed styles and the render tree.
3. AngleSharp.Renderer converts the tree into a display list and rasterizes it with Skia.

```cs
using AngleSharp;
using AngleSharp.Css;
using AngleSharp.Renderer;

var device = new DefaultRenderDevice { ViewPortWidth = 800, ViewPortHeight = 600 };
var context = BrowsingContext.New(Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRenderDevice(device).WithRendering());
var document = await context.OpenAsync(request => request.Content("<html><body>Hello</body></html>"));

var image = document.RenderToPng();
```

### The Render Device

The renderer takes the viewport from AngleSharp.Css's `IRenderDevice`, the same object that media queries are evaluated against:

- `ViewPortWidth` and `ViewPortHeight` are the size of the viewport, and so of the image.
- `FontSize` is the default font size (`medium`, the size `rem` refers to).
- The other properties (`Resolution`, `ColorBits`, ...) feed media queries; images are always rendered at one device pixel per CSS pixel.

Register it once with `WithRenderDevice(device)`, or pass it to a single call with `new HtmlRenderer().RenderToPng(document, device)`. Without a render device, a document renders in an 800×600 viewport (`HtmlRenderer.FallbackViewportWidth`/`FallbackViewportHeight`). The interactive harness and the geometry APIs (`GetBoundingClientRect`, ...) still need a registered device, since AngleSharp.Css evaluates `window.innerWidth` and the media queries of computed styles against it.

### Canvas Support

The renderer can also be configured to expose a basic 2D drawing context for `<canvas>` elements. Register the rendering service once on the browsing context with `Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRendering()` and then resolve the context through `canvas.GetContext("2d")`.

```cs
using AngleSharp;
using AngleSharp.Renderer;

var context = BrowsingContext.New(Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRendering());
var document = await context.OpenAsync(request => request.Content("<html><body><canvas width='120' height='80'></canvas></body></html>"));

var canvas = document.QuerySelector("canvas") as IHtmlCanvasElement;
var canvasContext = canvas?.GetContext("2d") as Canvas2DRenderingContext;

canvasContext?.SetFillStyle("#ff0000");
canvasContext?.FillRect(10f, 10f, 80f, 40f);
```

This implementation is intentionally lightweight and bitmap-backed, but it supports common operations such as rectangles, paths, text, clear operations, and save/restore state.

### Text And Fonts

The renderer supports text styling such as font size, weight, italic, alignment, letter and word spacing, `text-transform`, decorations, shadows, `white-space`, `word-break`, `overflow-wrap`, and `text-overflow`.
Inline content is laid out in line boxes, so nested inline elements keep their own styles, share a baseline with the surrounding text, and wrap together with it.

Generic font families like `serif`, `sans-serif`, and `monospace` always map to fonts bundled with the renderer, so they render the same on every machine.
Named families resolve only when installed on the host (or declared via `@font-face`), so prefer generic families when you need predictable output in visual tests.

Text is shaped with HarfBuzz, so kerning and ligatures (`fi`, `fl`) apply, Arabic letters join, and complex scripts such as Devanagari form their conjuncts.
`font-feature-settings`, `font-kerning`, `font-variant-ligatures` and `font-variant-numeric` select the OpenType features of the font; a non-zero `letter-spacing` turns optional ligatures off.
The bundled fonts cover Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic (DejaVu) and Devanagari (Noto Sans Devanagari, used only as a fallback); other scripts need an installed font or an `@font-face` that covers them.

### Visual Testing

The test suite uses PNG snapshots under `verification-assets/`. Missing baselines are created automatically unless strict mode is enabled with `ANGLESHARP_SNAPSHOT_STRICT=1`.


---

## Interactivity, Transitions & Animations (AngleSharp.Renderer)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/general/interactivity/
> Project: AngleSharp.Renderer (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Renderer)
> Package: AngleSharp.Renderer 0.12.0 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Renderer`
> Docs revision: 0a71fb1145856a0e638852edb3b9de0385eb01fa

`HtmlRenderer.RenderToPng`/`BuildDisplayList` render one static snapshot of a document by
themselves. To simulate mouse hover, drive CSS `transition`s and `animation`s, or read/set scroll
position, a document needs an **interactive DOM harness** - a small piece of state, bound to the
document's browsing context, that tracks things a real browser would (cursor position, scroll
offsets, a running clock) and feeds them back into rendering.

### Getting A Harness

A harness needs an `IRenderDevice` registered on the browsing context, then is created (or
retrieved, if one already exists) via `GetDomHarness()`:

```cs
using AngleSharp;
using AngleSharp.Css;
using AngleSharp.Renderer;

var renderDevice = new DefaultRenderDevice { ViewPortWidth = 320, ViewPortHeight = 200 };
var context = BrowsingContext.New(Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRenderDevice(renderDevice));
var document = await context.OpenAsync(request => request.Content(html));

var harness = document.Context.GetDomHarness();
```

Every document not wired up this way renders exactly as before - the interactive machinery is a
no-op until a harness exists for that browsing context.

### Simulating `:hover`

Set `MousePosition` in viewport coordinates. The harness hit-tests the layout, forces the
`:hover` pseudo-class on the topmost element under the cursor *and its whole ancestor chain*
(matching how a real pointer makes `.card:hover .title` work, not just the innermost element), and
raises `PaintInvalidated`:

```cs
harness.MousePosition = (50, 40);
var image = harness.PaintToPng();
```

`harness.HoveredElement` exposes the currently hit-tested element if you need it directly.

### Selecting Text

Text can be selected as in a browser. A host forwards the pointer to the harness - after firing
`mousedown`, unless that was canceled:

```cs
harness.BeginTextSelection(x, y);             // pressed; clickCount: 2 selects a word, 3 a paragraph
harness.ExtendTextSelection(x, y);            // moved with the button held
harness.EndTextSelection();                   // released

var text = harness.SelectedText;              // as shown, e.g., for the clipboard
```

`BeginTextSelection` takes `extend: true` for a press with Shift held, and returns false when
nothing can be selected there. `SelectAllText()` is for Ctrl+A and `ClearTextSelection()` removes
the selection. `PaintInvalidated` is raised when the selection changes; showing it needs no layout,
as `UpdateFrame()` returns the last frame with the selection painted.

The selection also is the DOM's: `document.GetSelection()` (`getSelection()` for scripts) has the
members of the [Selection API](https://w3c.github.io/selection-api/) except `modify`, and its changes are painted just
the same. `selectstart` (cancelable) and `selectionchange` are fired. `user-select` is honored
(`none`, `text`, `all`), what form controls show cannot be selected, and `::selection` gives the colors
of the highlight and the text.

A host shows the cursor of text where `frame.HasTextAt(x, y)` is true, which does not touch the DOM.

Selecting is on by default. It can be turned off for a document that has no use for it, in which case
layouts do not record where their text comes from:

```cs
harness.IsTextSelectionEnabled = false;
```

### Selecting Text Headlessly

No pointer is needed to select text, e.g. to highlight search hits in a screenshot or to test what a
selection covers. Select through the DOM and render; the harness only has to exist, since a document
without one paints no selection:

```cs
var device = new DefaultRenderDevice { ViewPortWidth = 400, ViewPortHeight = 200 };
var context = BrowsingContext.New(Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRenderDevice(device));
var document = await context.OpenAsync(request => request.Content("<p id='intro'>Hello World</p>"));
var harness = document.Context.GetDomHarness();

var text = document.GetElementById("intro")!.FirstChild!;
var selection = document.GetSelection();
selection.SetBaseAndExtent(text, 6, text, 11);    // "World"

var image = document.RenderToPng();               // with the highlight
```

Any way of the Selection API selects: `SelectAllChildren(element)`, `Collapse`/`Extend`, or
`AddRange` with a range from `document.CreateRange()`. `RemoveAllRanges()` takes the highlight away
again.

`selection.ToString()` and `harness.SelectedText` are the selected text as it is shown (collapsed
white space, `text-transform`, line breaks between blocks), i.e., what a browser copies to the
clipboard. Without a harness, `ToString()` is the text of the selected nodes.

Where it is comes from the range: `selection.GetRangeAt(0).GetClientRects()` gives a rectangle per
line box, and `GetBoundingClientRect()` the one around them, both in viewport coordinates.

The pointer gestures above work headlessly too, at coordinates of your choosing. For example, a
double click selects the word under the point:

```cs
harness.BeginTextSelection(30, 15, clickCount: 2);
harness.EndTextSelection();
var word = harness.SelectedText;
```

### Frames and Their Metrics

An interactive host lays out a frame with `PrepareFrame()` and rasterizes it on any thread, as it
no longer refers to the DOM. Every frame tells what its layout took, e.g., to show it in the
developer tools of a browser:

```cs
var frame = harness.PrepareFrame();
var metrics = frame.Metrics;

Console.WriteLine($"styles {metrics.Style}, boxes {metrics.Layout}, hit testing {metrics.HitTesting}");
Console.WriteLine($"{metrics.Elements} elements, {metrics.Boxes} boxes, {metrics.TrialLayouts} trial layouts");
```

`Total` is the sum of the phases: `Setup` (web fonts and the page's default text style), `Style`
(the render tree, i.e., matching selectors and the cascade), `Layout` (the boxes and what is painted),
`HitTesting` and `Subframes` (the documents of iframes). The counters tell how much work that was:
`StyleMaps`, `TextMeasurements`, `Commands` (of the display list), `HitTestEntries` and the
`AllocatedBytes`. A frame patched by `UpdateFrame()` is `IsIncremental`, and a frame moved with
`Reposition` needed no layout at all: its metrics are `RenderMetrics.None`.

A change of an element's state, i.e., hovering or focusing it, is often confined to it: only what
a selector of that state refers to (e.g., `.card:hover .title`) is styled again, and a change of
its colors, backgrounds, borders, outlines, shadows or text decoration is painted again without
laying out anything, so `UpdateFrame()` patches the last frame (keeping its hit-test map, unless a
`cursor` changed). Selectors that style other elements with the state, like `.tip:hover + .note`
or the rules of a shadow tree, still lay out the document again. The harness knows the hovered
element, while a host that moves the focus tells it so:

```cs
field.DoFocus();
harness.NotifyStateChanged(field);
var frame = harness.UpdateFrame() ?? harness.PrepareFrame();
```

A page that was just loaded can be shown early on: `PrepareViewportFrame()` styles and lays out
only what is in the viewport (with the overscan). If the page goes on below, the frame is
`IsPartial`: its `ContentHeight` and hit-test map end there, and it is animating, as the next
frame lays out the whole page. Reading the geometry (e.g., `getBoundingClientRect`) lays it out as
well, and `UpdateFrame()` doesn't patch a partial frame:

```cs
var first = harness.PrepareViewportFrame();
// show it, then
var frame = first.IsPartial ? harness.PrepareFrame() : first;
```

Images of a page (e.g., `RenderToPng`) are rendered the same way. A document whose generated
content uses CSS counters or quotes (with elements they apply to) is styled as a whole, as these
depend on all elements before.

For a large document, the computed styles of its elements are read on all cores (as AngleSharp.Css
matches their selectors), while the DOM is not changed. A host without cores to spare turns this off:

```cs
AppContext.SetSwitch("AngleSharp.Renderer.DisableParallelism", true);
AppContext.SetSwitch("AngleSharp.Css.DisableParallelism", true);
```

### The Virtual Clock

There is no real-time timer anywhere in this renderer. CSS `transition`s and `animation`s are both
measured against a virtual clock that only moves when you tell it to, via `AdvanceTime`:

```cs
harness.AdvanceTime(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500));
var midFrame = harness.PaintToPng();
```

Call `AdvanceTime` with however much time you want a frame to represent, then paint - repeating
that pair of calls is how you produce a sequence of frames (for example, to assemble a GIF or
video of an animation) instead of only ever the resting/end states.

An interactive host gets the frames of animations cheaply from `UpdateFrame()` after `AdvanceTime`:
when the animations and transitions only change the `transform`, `opacity` or `filter` of boxes (or
what boxes paint of their own, e.g. a background color), the last frame is painted with the new
values without a layout. Otherwise `UpdateFrame()` returns null, and `PrepareFrame()` lays out the
document:

```cs
harness.AdvanceTime(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(16));
var frame = harness.UpdateFrame() ?? harness.PrepareFrame();
```

A frame with sticky boxes can be moved to another scroll position as well (`CanReposition`): the
sticky boxes stick there anew, also for its `HitTestMap`.

### CSS `transition`

A `transition` animates a property when its own natural value changes for some other reason: a
`:hover` state change, or anything changing the style of an element between two frames (e.g. a
script adding a class). An element seen for the first time (just inserted, or no longer
`display: none`) has no transition, like in a browser:

```cs
var html = """
<html>
  <head>
    <style>
      #box { width: 40px; height: 40px; background-color: blue; transition: background-color 1s ease; }
      #box:hover { background-color: red; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body><div id="box"></div></body>
</html>
""";

var harness = document.Context.GetDomHarness();
harness.MousePosition = (20, 20); // hovers #box, starts the transition
harness.AdvanceTime(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500)); // halfway through the 1s duration

var midway = harness.PaintToPng(); // background is purple, not yet fully red
```

Moving the pointer away mid-transition reverses it smoothly from whatever is currently on screen,
with its own full declared duration - not a jump back to blue, and not just the remaining
fraction of the original 1s.

Like animations, transitions tell the element about themselves once a frame is painted:
`transitionrun` (when it is created), `transitionstart` (once its delay is over), `transitionend`
and `transitioncancel` (replaced or removed before it ended) are dispatched as `TransitionEvent`s,
with the `propertyName` and the `elapsedTime` in seconds. A property that is not interpolated here
(see below; e.g. `max-height` or `visibility`) still has these events, while its value changes
right away; a shorthand like `padding` or `border-color` transitions its longhands.

### CSS `animation`/`@keyframes`

An `animation` needs no trigger at all - one in the first frame of a document is pinned to
virtual-clock zero (matching a real browser's "starts playing at page load"), one an element gets
later (e.g. by a class a script adds) starts at the time of the frame that finds it, and either
keeps looping per `animation-iteration-count`:

```cs
var html = """
<html>
  <head>
    <style>
      @keyframes fade {
        0% { opacity: 0; }
        100% { opacity: 1; }
      }
      #box { width: 40px; height: 40px; background-color: blue; animation: fade 2s linear; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body><div id="box"></div></body>
</html>
""";

var harness = document.Context.GetDomHarness();
harness.AdvanceTime(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1000)); // halfway through the 2s duration

var midway = harness.PaintToPng(); // #box is 50% opaque
```

`animation-name` (including multiple, comma-separated animations on one element),
`-duration`, `-delay`, `-timing-function` (`ease`/`linear`/`cubic-bezier()`/`steps()`),
`-iteration-count` (a number, or `infinite`), `-direction` (`normal`/`reverse`/`alternate`/
`alternate-reverse`), and `-fill-mode` (`none`/`forwards`/`backwards`/`both`) are all supported.
`animation-play-state: paused` freezes an animation where it is, and the time it is paused does
not count.

The frames tell the element about its animations, like a browser: once a frame (or a picture) is
painted, `animationstart`, `animationiteration`, `animationend` and `animationcancel` (an
animation the element no longer names before it ended) are dispatched as `AnimationEvent`s, with
the `animationName` and the `elapsedTime` in seconds. With an event loop they are a task of it,
else they are dispatched right after painting. Pages often wait for `animationend` before going
on, e.g. to show the next view of a form.

```cs
box.AddEventListener("animationend", (_, ev) => Console.WriteLine(((AnimationEvent)ev).AnimationName));
harness.PrepareFrame();                            // animationstart
harness.AdvanceTime(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
harness.PrepareFrame();                            // animationend: "fade"
```

### What Can Be Animated

Both `transition` and `animation` only ever interpolate a fixed set of properties:

- **Colors** (channel-wise): `background-color`, `color`, `border-top-color`,
  `border-right-color`, `border-bottom-color`, `border-left-color`
- **Numeric lengths/`opacity`** (plain numeric lerp): `opacity`, `width`, `height`, `font-size`,
  `margin-top`/`-right`/`-bottom`/`-left`, `padding-top`/`-right`/`-bottom`/`-left`,
  `border-top-width`/`-right-width`/`-bottom-width`/`-left-width`, `top`, `left`, `right`, `bottom`
- **Function lists** (function by function): `transform`, `translate`, `rotate`, `scale`,
  `filter`, `backdrop-filter`

`transition-property: all` and any other property named in a `@keyframes` block are limited to
this same list; other properties change right away (a transition of one still has its events).

### Animated Images

A GIF or WebP of several frames plays without a layout: rasterizing a frame shows the image's frame
whose time has come, from the moment the image was first painted, as often as the image loops (the
wall clock, not the virtual one). `GetTimeToNextImageFrame()` tells when an animated image in or near
the viewport of the frame changes next, so a host knows when to rasterize it again:

```cs
var frame = harness.PrepareFrame();
var pixels = frame.Rasterize();

if (frame.GetTimeToNextImageFrame() is { } delay)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay);
    pixels = frame.Rasterize();                    // the next frame of the GIF
}
```

### Media Controls

An `audio` element with the `controls` attribute is painted with the controls of Chrome (300x54 by
default): a play/pause button, the time, a timeline and a mute button, showing the state of the
element (`paused`, `currentTime`, `duration`, `muted`). While the media plays, the time and the
timeline are painted for the moment the frame is rasterized, so they go on without a layout, and
`GetTimeToNextImageFrame()` also tells when they change next. Without `controls`, an `audio` element
is not rendered.

The controls are painted, not boxes, so a host finds the part a press is on, in viewport
coordinates, and acts on the element itself:

```cs
switch (audio.GetMediaControlAt(x, y))
{
    case MediaControlPart.PlayPause:
        // play() or pause(), depending on audio.IsPaused
        break;
    case MediaControlPart.Mute:
        audio.IsMuted = !audio.IsMuted;
        break;
    case MediaControlPart.Timeline:
        audio.CurrentTime = audio.GetMediaTimelinePosition(x)!.Value * audio.Duration;
        break;
}
```

### Input Pickers

The `color`, `date`, `datetime-local`, `month`, `time` and `week` inputs open a picker as in a
browser: a color picker (saturation and brightness area, hue slider, the suggestions of the input's
`list` or a few common colors), a calendar (of days, weeks with their ISO numbers, or months; with
columns of hours, minutes and AM/PM for `datetime-local`), or the columns of a time. Like the list of
a dropdown (`SelectPopup`), a picker is not part of the layout: a host opens it, shows it on top of a
frame and forwards the pointer and the keyboard to it, in viewport coordinates:

```cs
var picker = input.OpenInputPicker();          // null if the input has none, or is disabled or read-only
frame = frame.WithOverlay(picker.Render());

// a press on the picker; a press anywhere else closes it with picker.Close()
var result = picker.PointerDown(x, y);
// also PointerMove, PointerUp, Wheel(x, y, deltaY) and KeyDown("ArrowLeft", "Enter", "Escape", ...)

switch (result)
{
    case InputPickerResult.Repaint:
        frame = frame.WithOverlay(picker.Render());
        break;
    case InputPickerResult.Close:
        // hide the picker
        break;
}
```

Choosing sets the input's value and fires `input`; `change` is fired when the picker closes with a
value other than the one it opened with. `picker.Close(cancel: true)` (and Escape) brings that value
back. `min`, `max` and `step` disable what they don't allow: days, weeks or months off the step
(counted from `min`, else the `value` attribute) are greyed out, and the time columns only list
the hours, minutes and seconds the step allows (a seconds column appears when the step isn't a
whole number of minutes); a chosen time moves to the nearest allowed one. `step="any"` allows
everything. `InputValueConstraints.For(input)` gives custom pickers the same rules. The picker follows the color scheme of the
input (as the list of a dropdown does) and its `accent-color`. `InputPickerOptions` sets where the
viewport of the input's document is (for an input in an iframe), the page's device and the current
time, which marks today and is shown when the input has no value.

#### Custom Controls

How an input is shown is up to its `IInputControl`: `GetIntrinsicSize` gives its size when `width`
or `height` is `auto`, `Paint` paints the content of the input (its border, padding and background
come from the style sheets) and `CreatePicker` creates its picker. A size is of the content box
(padding and border are added, as for a text field) or of the border box
(`InputControlSizeBox.BorderBox`, as for the swatch of a color input); a side left null, or a null
size, is the built-in one of the type. The built-in ones are
`ColorInputControl` and `DateTimeInputControl` with the pickers `ColorPicker`, `CalendarPicker` and
`TimePicker`; all of them can be derived from. Another control is registered with the configuration,
for any input type:

```cs
var config = Configuration.Default
    .WithCss()
    .WithRenderDevice(device)
    .WithInputControl("color", new MyColorControl());   // the other types keep the built-in controls

sealed class MyColorControl : ColorInputControl
{
    public override InputControlSize? GetIntrinsicSize(InputControlSizeContext context) =>
        new(context.MeasureText("#000000") + 40f, context.LineHeight);

    public override void Paint(InputControlPaintContext context)
    {
        // what to paint, in the coordinates of context.DisplayList
        context.DisplayList.FillRect(context.ContentBox, MyColors.Parse(context.Value));
        context.DrawText(context.Value, context.ContentBox.X + 4f, context.TextBaseline);
    }

    public override IInputPicker? CreatePicker(InputPickerContext context) => new MyColorPicker(context);
}
```

`InputControlPaintContext` measures and paints text as the input's text is painted (`MeasureText`,
`DrawText`). `InputPickerContext` gives the input's place in the viewport (`Anchor`, and `Place` for
putting a picker below or above it), its font, the colors of its scheme (`Palette`) and a text
measurer. Deriving from `InputPicker` brings setting the value with its events (`SetValue`,
`Choose`), closing, and painting text in the input's font. `WithInputControls(provider)` replaces
the registry with any `IInputControlProvider`; returning null for an input leaves it to the
built-in control of its type, if any. The painting happens during layout, so it must only depend on
the state of the input.

### Scrolling

The same harness also tracks per-element scroll position, read and set through the standard
CSSOM-view properties/methods (`element.scrollTop`, `element.scrollTo(...)`,
`element.scrollIntoView()`, ...) - `RenderToPng`/`BuildDisplayList` honor whatever scroll position
is currently set once a harness exists for the document.


---

## API Documentation (AngleSharp.Renderer)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/tutorials/api/
> Project: AngleSharp.Renderer (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Renderer)
> Package: AngleSharp.Renderer 0.12.0 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Renderer`
> Docs revision: 0a71fb1145856a0e638852edb3b9de0385eb01fa

### Configuration

A browsing context needs AngleSharp.Css and a render device. `WithRendering()` adds the services for `<canvas>` (its 2D context) and for `<img>` data. The renderer loads the image of an `<img>` it lays out (the source its render node picked for the device from `srcset`, `sizes` and the sources of a `<picture>`, see `ElementRenderNode.ImageSource`), as AngleSharp's image element requests nothing by itself; a render waits for it, while a frame of an interactive harness paints it once it has loaded, and loads a lazy one (`loading=lazy`, with scripting) only once it is within 1250px of the viewport and of the scroll containers around it. Its natural size (also `naturalWidth` and `naturalHeight`) is divided by the density of the picked candidate (e.g. `2x`). An image not in a document (e.g. `new Image()` of a script) is loaded once it has a source:

```cs
using AngleSharp;
using AngleSharp.Css;
using AngleSharp.Renderer;

var device = new DefaultRenderDevice { ViewPortWidth = 1024, ViewPortHeight = 768, FontSize = 16 };
var config = Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRenderDevice(device).WithRendering();
var context = BrowsingContext.New(config);
```

The render device's `ViewPortWidth` and `ViewPortHeight` are the size of the viewport, and so of the rendered image (800×600 when the context has no render device); `FontSize` is the default font size. Images are rendered at one device pixel per CSS pixel.

### Rendering A Document

`document.RenderToPng()` renders the viewport of a document with the render device of its context:

```cs
var image = document.RenderToPng();
File.WriteAllBytes("page.png", image.Data);
```

`HtmlRenderer` is the same with more control: it takes a render device per call, and its constructors take an `IRenderBackend` (default: `SkiaRenderBackend`) and an `ITextMeasurer` (the backend, if it is one):

```cs
var renderer = new HtmlRenderer();
var image = renderer.RenderToPng(document, new DefaultRenderDevice { ViewPortWidth = 320, ViewPortHeight = 200 });
var displayList = renderer.BuildDisplayList(document);
```

A render shows the page at its current scroll position once the document has an interactive harness (see [Interactivity](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/general/interactivity/index.html.md)), and at the top otherwise. `RenderToPng` is `RenderToImage` with the default options.

### Render Options

`RenderToImage` takes `RenderOptions`, modeled on the screenshots of browser automation tools:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FullPage` | `false` | The whole page, from its top to the end of its content, instead of the viewport at its scroll position. The image is as wide as the viewport. |
| `Clip` | none | A `RenderRect` of the page in CSS pixels, from the top left of the page (the scroll position plays no role). Limited to the page and the viewport's width. |
| `DeviceScaleFactor` | `1` | Device pixels per CSS pixel, e.g. `2` for a HiDPI image. The layout stays the same; text, borders and SVG are painted sharp at the higher resolution. |
| `OmitBackground` | `false` | Leaves out the white behind the page, so the image is transparent where the page paints no background. |
| `Format` | `Png` | `Png`, `Jpeg` (transparent areas become white) or `Webp`. |
| `Quality` | `90` | The quality of JPEG and WebP, from 0 to 100. |

```cs
var page = document.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { FullPage = true });
var retina = document.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { DeviceScaleFactor = 2f });
var thumbnail = document.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { Format = RenderImageFormat.Jpeg, Quality = 80 });
var banner = document.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { Clip = new RenderRect(0, 0, 800, 120) });
```

An element renders its border box, wherever it is on the page; a `Clip` is then relative to the border box:

```cs
var card = document.QuerySelector(".card")!;
var image = card.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { DeviceScaleFactor = 2f, OmitBackground = true });
```

A capture beyond the viewport is still laid out in the viewport: viewport units and media queries keep their values, and `position: fixed` boxes are painted once, at the top of the page. `HtmlRenderer.RenderToPixels(document, options)` gives the same capture as raw pixels. Rendering with options does not create the interactive harness; when the document has one, the selection is painted as well.

### RenderedImage And RenderedPixels

`RenderedImage` is an encoded image: `Data` (the PNG bytes), `Width`, `Height` and `MimeType`.

For raw pixels, use `renderer.RenderToPixels(document, options)`, rasterize a display list with a backend implementing `IPixelRenderBackend`, or rasterize a frame of the harness with `frame.Rasterize()`. `RenderedPixels` holds premultiplied RGBA bytes, `RowBytes` (`Width * 4`) per row:

```cs
using AngleSharp.Renderer.Rendering;
using AngleSharp.Renderer.Skia;

var backend = new SkiaRenderBackend();
var pixels = backend.RenderToPixels(renderer.BuildDisplayList(document), new RenderViewport(1024, 768));
```

### DisplayList

`DisplayList` is the backend-agnostic result of layout: a flat list of `RenderCommand`s in paint order (`displayList.Commands`), plus the web fonts it uses (`Fonts`). Inspect it to debug layout without rasterizing, or paint it with a backend of your own.

- Drawing: `FillRectCommand` (backgrounds, borders, outlines; colors, gradients and images as `RenderPaint`), `StrokeRoundedRectCommand`, `FillRingCommand`, `DrawTextCommand`, `DrawTextShadowCommand`, `DrawBoxShadowCommand`, `DrawImageCommand`, `DrawBorderImageCommand`, `DrawBackdropFilterCommand` and `DrawSubframeCommand` (iframes).
- Scopes, as `Push…`/`Pop…` pairs that nest: clips (`PushClipCommand`, `PushClipShapeCommand`), transforms, opacity, filters, blend modes, masks and viewport anchors (fixed boxes).

A custom backend implements `IRenderBackend.RenderToPng(displayList, viewport)` (and `IPixelRenderBackend.RenderToPixels` for raw pixels). Layout measures text with the `ITextMeasurer` given to `HtmlRenderer`; pass the measurer of the fonts your backend paints with, or lines break differently from what is drawn.

### Geometry

With a render device registered, the [CSSOM View](https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom-view/) APIs answer from the layout, in viewport coordinates:

```cs
var rect = element.GetBoundingClientRect();          // also GetClientRects()
var width = element.GetOffsetWidth();                 // GetClientWidth(), GetScrollHeight(), ...
var hit = document.ElementFromPoint(100, 40);         // ElementsFromPoint for the whole stack
var caret = document.CaretPositionFromPoint(100, 40); // text node and offset
var textRect = range.GetBoundingClientRect();         // rects of a DOM range, e.g. a word
```

Scrolling goes through `element.ScrollTo(...)`, `SetScrollTop(...)`, `ScrollIntoView(...)` and `window.ScrollTo(...)`. `ResizeObserver` and `IntersectionObserver` report changes as the frames are laid out.

### Selection

`document.GetSelection()` (and `window.GetSelection()`) is the DOM's [Selection](https://w3c.github.io/selection-api/), painted in rendered images once the document has a harness. See [Selecting Text Headlessly](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/general/interactivity/index.html.md#selecting-text-headlessly).

### Animations

CSS transitions and animations run on a virtual clock (`harness.AdvanceTime(...)`). The Web Animations API is there as well: `element.Animate(keyframes, options)` returns an `Animation`, and `element.GetAnimations()`/`document.GetAnimations()` list them. See [Interactivity](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/general/interactivity/index.html.md).

### Fonts

`document.Fonts()` is the document's `FontFaceSet` of the [CSS Font Loading API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-font-loading/): the faces of its `@font-face` rules, and faces added from code (from a `url(...)` or the bytes of a font). Adding a face loads it (browsers wait until text uses it), and `Ready` settles once the faces being loaded are done:

```cs
var face = new DocumentFontFace(document.DefaultView!, "Brand", fontBytes);
document.Fonts().Add(face);
await document.Fonts().Ready;
```

A face that fails to load stays in the set (its `Status` is `error`) and the text falls back to the next family. Faces of `@font-face` rules are in the set too, but cannot be added or deleted.

Generic families (`serif`, `sans-serif`, `monospace`, ...) always use the bundled fonts, so they render the same on every machine.

### Canvas Rendering Context

With `WithRendering()`, `<canvas>` elements have a 2D context backed by Skia. The members of the [canvas API](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html) are available as methods: rectangles, paths (`Arc`, `ArcTo`, `Ellipse`, `RoundRect`, Bézier curves), `Fill`/`Stroke`/`Clip` with fill rules, text (`FillText`, `StrokeText`, `MeasureText`), `DrawImage`, gradients (linear, radial, conic), patterns, transforms, line dashes, shadows, compositing, hit tests (`IsPointInPath`) and `Save`/`Restore`. Properties are `Get…`/`Set…` methods:

```cs
var canvas = document.QuerySelector("canvas") as IHtmlCanvasElement;
var canvasContext = canvas?.GetContext("2d") as Canvas2DRenderingContext;

canvasContext?.SetFillStyle("#00ff00");
canvasContext?.FillRect(10f, 10f, 80f, 40f);
var png = canvasContext?.ToImage("image/png");
```

A canvas in a page shows its bitmap when the page is rendered.


---

## Examples (AngleSharp.Renderer)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/tutorials/examples/
> Project: AngleSharp.Renderer (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Renderer)
> Package: AngleSharp.Renderer 0.12.0 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Renderer`
> Docs revision: 0a71fb1145856a0e638852edb3b9de0385eb01fa

### Render A Page To PNG

```cs
using AngleSharp;
using AngleSharp.Css;
using AngleSharp.Renderer;

var device = new DefaultRenderDevice { ViewPortWidth = 320, ViewPortHeight = 200, FontSize = 16 };
var context = BrowsingContext.New(Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRenderDevice(device));
var document = await context.OpenAsync(request => request.Content("""
<html>
	<body>
		<p style="font-family:serif; font-size:24px;">Hello renderer</p>
	</body>
</html>
"""));

var image = document.RenderToPng();

File.WriteAllBytes("render.png", image.Data);
```

### Capture The Full Page, An Element, Or A HiDPI Image

```cs
File.WriteAllBytes("page.png", document.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { FullPage = true }).Data);

var intro = document.QuerySelector("p")!;
File.WriteAllBytes("paragraph@2x.png", intro.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { DeviceScaleFactor = 2f }).Data);

var preview = document.RenderToImage(new RenderOptions { Format = RenderImageFormat.Webp, Quality = 75 });
File.WriteAllBytes("preview.webp", preview.Data);
```

### Highlight A Search Hit

Selecting text needs no pointer: select a DOM range and render. The selection is painted once the document has a harness (see [Interactivity](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/general/interactivity/index.html.md#selecting-text-headlessly)):

```cs
var harness = document.Context.GetDomHarness();
var paragraph = document.QuerySelector("p")!;
var text = paragraph.FirstChild!;
var start = text.TextContent.IndexOf("renderer", StringComparison.Ordinal);

document.GetSelection().SetBaseAndExtent(text, start, text, start + "renderer".Length);

File.WriteAllBytes("highlighted.png", document.RenderToPng().Data);
```

### Draw To A Canvas

```cs
using AngleSharp;
using AngleSharp.Renderer;
using AngleSharp.Html.Dom;

var context = BrowsingContext.New(Configuration.Default.WithCss().WithRendering());
var document = await context.OpenAsync(request => request.Content("""
<html>
	<body>
		<canvas width="120" height="80"></canvas>
	</body>
</html>
"""));

var canvas = document.QuerySelector("canvas") as IHtmlCanvasElement;
var canvasContext = canvas?.GetContext("2d") as Canvas2DRenderingContext;

canvasContext?.SetFillStyle("#ff0000");
canvasContext?.FillRect(10f, 10f, 100f, 50f);
canvasContext?.SetFillStyle("#00ff00");
canvasContext?.FillRect(30f, 20f, 50f, 30f);

var png = canvasContext?.ToImage("image/png");
File.WriteAllBytes("canvas.png", png ?? Array.Empty<byte>());
```

`ToImage` encodes the canvas bitmap (`image/png`, `image/jpeg` or `image/webp`).

### Compare Different Font Families

```html
<p style="font-family:serif;">Serif sample</p>
<p style="font-family:sans-serif;">Sans sample</p>
<p style="font-family:monospace;">Mono sample</p>
```

Use this pattern when you want visual tests to prove that generic families are mapped correctly.

### Inspect The Display List

```cs
var renderer = new HtmlRenderer();
var displayList = renderer.BuildDisplayList(document);

foreach (var command in displayList.Commands)
{
	Console.WriteLine(command);
}
```

Inspecting the display list is often the fastest way to debug box-model or text-layout behavior.

## Questions (AngleSharp.Renderer)

> Source: https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/renderer/tutorials/questions/
> Project: AngleSharp.Renderer (https://github.com/AngleSharp/AngleSharp.Renderer)
> Package: AngleSharp.Renderer 0.12.0 — install with `dotnet add package AngleSharp.Renderer`
> Docs revision: 0a71fb1145856a0e638852edb3b9de0385eb01fa

### Why do web-safe fonts look the same on my machine?

The renderer maps generic families such as `serif`, `sans-serif`, and `monospace` to fonts bundled with it (DejaVu), not to installed fonts, so they look the same on every machine.

Named families (e.g. `Arial`) resolve only when installed on the host or declared via `@font-face`; otherwise the next entry of the `font-family` list is used.

### Why does my text in another script show boxes?

Characters the resolved font has no glyph for fall back to the next `font-family` entry, then the bundled fonts (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari), then whatever the host has installed. For other scripts (e.g. Thai or CJK) declare an `@font-face` or install a font that covers them.

### Why does a snapshot fail when I add a new baseline?

Visual snapshots compare the current PNG against the baseline in `verification-assets/`. If the baseline is missing, it is created automatically unless strict mode is enabled.

### How do I debug layout issues?

Start with `BuildDisplayList(...)` and inspect the commands before rasterizing. This usually makes it easier to see whether the issue is in layout, text measurement, or final drawing.

### Can I render only the render tree?

Yes. AngleSharp.Css exposes the render tree via `window.Render(...)`, which is helpful when you want to inspect computed styles before handing the document to AngleSharp.Renderer.


---

### Recommended Reading Order

If you are new to AngleSharp.Browser, this order gives a practical ramp-up:

1. [Getting Started](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/general/basics/index.html.md) for setup and first working code.
2. [Examples](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/tutorials/examples/index.html.md) for copy-paste recipes.
3. [Avalonia Control](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/general/avalonia/index.html.md) if you want to show pages in a desktop application.
4. [Browser Engine](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/general/engine/index.html.md) and [Configuration](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/general/configuration/index.html.md) to understand threading, navigation and profiles.
5. [Rendering](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/general/rendering/index.html.md), [Input](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/general/input/index.html.md) and [Writing a Custom Host](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/tutorials/custom-host/index.html.md) to integrate another UI framework.
6. [API Documentation](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/tutorials/api/index.html.md) as a reference and the [FAQ](https://anglesharp.github.io/docs/browser/tutorials/questions/index.html.md) for common pitfalls.

### What You Can Do With AngleSharp.Browser

Typical use cases include:

- Taking screenshots of pages without a display, entirely in .NET.
- Driving pages in tests: clicking, typing, scrolling, and inspecting the DOM afterwards.
- Embedding a web view without a native browser dependency in an Avalonia application.
- Showing your own UI written in HTML and CSS, wired up with .NET event handlers.
- Building browser-like tools with history, profiles, multiple windows and diagnostics.
